/style-guide.title: Style guide — Margin
text_lines: Everything on the site comes from a handful of styles, four CMS collections and a few components. Change them and every page follows.
Site settings and the Header / Footer
Name, email, phone and navigation live in the Header and Footer components and the Main layout template. Edit them once; every page follows.

Signal, Signal 2 and Signal Text are the accent: change them in Assets → Colors and every highlight, button and tick follows. Ink, Fog, White, Slate and the Rule, Ink and Fog styles colour every line, border and muted text.
Display, Heading 1–4, Lead, Body, Label and Meta. Change the font or size once in Assets → Text and the whole site updates, per breakpoint.
Services, Case Studies, Insights and Team. Each entry becomes its own page; replace the sample content before you publish.

The client logos are the Logo Set component: edit them there and all three copies in the scrolling row follow. They spread across its width, so any number of logos keeps the loop seamless. The not-now card is the Not-now list component: on each instance set Label, Title, Item 1–5, State 1–5 (Keep, Stop or Off) and Summary.
Point the Pick a time button on Contact at your own Cal.com, Calendly or SavvyCal link.

The showcase photo starts where the arrow artwork ends, held by the Copy frame’s minimum height (392 on desktop, 356 on tablet, 352 on phone). If you resize or move the artwork, change these to match.

Effects come from MarginMotion in Assets → Code. They find their parts by layer name, so keep Arrow, Title, Hover photo, Track, Phases, Week and Bar if you restyle, and keep not-now rows as box, text and tag.
Dashed “Sample” pills mark invented figures, logos and quotes. Delete each one once its content is real.
A monochrome base and one accent.
Fraunces for headings, Geist for reading, Geist Mono for data.
We find the few decisions that matter and stay until they’re working.
Fixed fees, scoped to a decision and agreed in writing before we start.
Buttons, flags and the submit button are components with variants.

/work/fernhill.title: Fernhill: Repositioning a freight platform from “cheapest” to “most certain”. — Margin
text_lines: Repositioning a freight platform from “cheapest” to “most certain”.
Fernhill was winning deals on price and losing them on renewal. We rebuilt its positioning around delivery certainty and retired two of its three target segments.

Fernhill had grown to $14M by being cheaper than the brokers it replaced, until two well-funded competitors got cheaper still. A third of new customers churned within a year. The leadership team wanted to cut price again; the board wanted a new market. Nobody had looked closely at the customers who stayed.
Listened to the ones who stayed
Fourteen interviews. The loyal customers never mentioned price. They talked about knowing where their freight was without calling anyone.
Mid-sized manufacturers with time-critical freight renewed at twice the rate of everyone else. We built for them and stopped chasing the rest.
‘Cheapest’ became ‘most certain’, across the homepage, deck and first-call script, written with the people who had to use them.

Within two quarters qualified pipeline was up 41% while lead volume fell, and the sales cycle dropped from 94 to 73 days. The new market went on the not-now list with a trigger to reopen it. Fernhill hit the trigger a year later.
What they kept, and what they stopped.
“They asked the question our board had been circling for a year, then stayed long enough to help us answer it.”

/work/oakmont-health.title: Oakmont Health: Turning a founder-led sales team into a repeatable one. — Margin
text_lines: Turning a founder-led sales team into a repeatable one.
Every enterprise deal still needed the founder in the room. We wrote down how she actually sold and coached two account executives through their first solo closes.

Oakmont’s founder had closed all forty of its enterprise customers herself. She was very good at it, and she was the reason the company couldn’t grow past one new deal a month. Two experienced hires were losing deals she would have won, and nobody could say why.
Eleven recorded sales calls. The big difference: she qualified out a third of prospects in the first call.
A five-question qualification framework and a discovery script, in her words rather than a sales methodology’s.
The founder joined every call for a month, then every other call, then only when asked.
Within a year the enterprise win rate rose from 11% to 25%, and seven in ten deals closed without the founder on the call. She now spends her time on product and still reads every lost-deal note.
What they kept, and what they stopped.
“The diagnostic was ten pages long. Our leadership team still quotes it in meetings.”
Hiring a VP Sales in year one

/work/tidewater.title: Tidewater Studio: Raising fees by a third without losing a single client. — Margin
text_lines: Raising fees by a third without losing a single client.
Tidewater priced by the hour and competed on cost. We repackaged its work into three fixed-scope offers and rehearsed the conversation with every partner before the first renewal.

Tidewater’s work won awards; its fees didn’t reflect it. Every proposal was an hourly estimate, every estimate was negotiated down, and the partners were sure that raising prices would cost them the two clients who made up 40% of revenue.
A delayed planning approval cost clients more than Tidewater’s entire fee. That reframed every conversation that followed.
Three fixed-scope offers with clear inclusions and a short, honest list of exclusions.
Every partner practised the renewal conversation twice with us before having it with a client.

The average project fee rose from $120k to $160k across the next eleven proposals, and the win rate went up, not down. Both large clients renewed. One asked why they hadn’t been offered fixed fees years ago.
What they kept, and what they stopped.
“Nora talked us out of a rebrand. It was the most valuable thing anyone told us that year.”
Price the outcome, not the hours
